title: CTS Language Appreciation — Unit 9: Four More Greek Words — The Vocabulary of Salvation

blocks.en: Language Appreciation — Unit 9: Four More Greek Words — The Vocabulary of Salvation
blocks.es_reference: Apreciación de Lenguas Bíblicas — Unidad 9: Cuatro palabras griegas más — El vocabulario de la salvación

blocks.en: Unit 9 · Romans 1:16–17 · Pistis, Sôzô, Dikaiosynê, Kyrios
blocks.es_reference: Unidad 9 · Romanos 1:16–17 · Pistis, Sôzô, Dikaiosynê, Kyrios

blocks.en: Four More Greek Words — The Vocabulary of Salvation
blocks.es_reference: Cuatro palabras griegas más — El vocabulario de la salvación

blocks.en: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth … for therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith."
blocks.es_reference: «Porque no me avergüenzo del evangelio de Cristo, porque es el poder de Dios para salvación a todo aquel que cree … porque en el evangelio la justicia de Dios se revela de fe en fe, como está escrito: Mas el justo por la fe vivirá».

blocks.en: Unit Scripture: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith." — Romans 1:16–17 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Escritura de la Unidad: «Porque no me avergüenzo del evangelio de Cristo, porque es el poder de Dios para salvación a todo aquel que cree; al judío primeramente, y también al griego. Porque en el evangelio la justicia de Dios se revela de fe en fe, como está escrito: Mas el justo por la fe vivirá». — Romanos 1:16–17 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation: The Tower in Wittenberg
blocks.es_reference: Orientación: La torre en Wittenberg

blocks.en: In 1515 a young Augustinian monk named Martin Luther sat in his study in the tower of the Black Cloister at Wittenberg, preparing lectures on the Epistle to the Romans. He had spent his adult life trying to earn salvation. He had fasted until his body broke down. He had crawled up the Scala Sancta in Rome on bleeding knees. He had confessed his sins for six hours at a stretch until his confessor told him to go away and come back when he had committed real sins. He was a tortured soul, and the verse that tortured him most was Romans 1:17: "the righteousness of God is revealed."
blocks.es_reference: En 1515 un joven monje agustino llamado Martín Lutero estaba sentado en su estudio en la torre del Claustro Negro en Wittenberg, preparando lecciones sobre la Epístola a los Romanos. Había pasado su vida adulta tratando de ganar la salvación. Había ayunado hasta que su cuerpo colapsó. Había gateado por la Scala Sancta en Roma con rodillas sangrantes. Había confesado sus pecados durante seis horas seguidas hasta que su confesor le dijo que se fuera y volviera cuando hubiera cometido pecados verdaderos. Era un alma atormentada, y el versículo que más lo atormentaba era Romanos 1:17: «la justicia de Dios se revela».

blocks.en: The Latin word in his Bible was justitia Dei, "the justice of God." To Luther, the righteousness of God meant the perfect standard by which God would judge him and find him guilty. The verse read like a death sentence. How could that be good news? He hated the verse. He hated God for putting it in the Bible. And then, while he was preparing his lectures, he opened the Greek text Erasmus had published just months earlier in 1516, and he read the same verse in the language Paul actually wrote: dikaiosynê theou. He looked at the verb forms. He saw that dikaiosynê in Paul did not mean the standard by which God judges. It meant the righteousness God gives as a free gift to those who believe. The just shall live by faith. Not by works. Not by climbing stairs on bloody knees. By faith.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra latina en su Biblia era justitia Dei, «la justicia de Dios». Para Lutero, la justicia de Dios significaba el estándar perfecto por el cual Dios lo juzgaría y lo encontraría culpable. El versículo le sonaba como una sentencia de muerte. ¿Cómo podía eso ser buenas nuevas? Odiaba el versículo. Odiaba a Dios por ponerlo en la Biblia. Y entonces, mientras preparaba sus lecciones, abrió el texto griego que Erasmo había publicado apenas meses antes en 1516, y leyó el mismo versículo en el idioma en que Pablo realmente escribió: dikaiosynê theou. Miró las formas verbales. Vio que dikaiosynê en Pablo no significaba el estándar por el cual Dios juzga. Significaba la justicia que Dios da como un regalo gratuito a los que creen. El justo por la fe vivirá. Por la fe. No por obras. No por subir escaleras con rodillas sangrientas. Por la fe.

blocks.en: When Luther understood the Greek word dikaiosynê, he said it was as if "the gates of paradise opened and I walked in." That moment in the Wittenberg tower lit the Reformation.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Lutero entendió la palabra griega dikaiosynê, dijo que fue como si «las puertas del paraíso se abrieran y yo entrara». Ese momento en la torre de Wittenberg encendió la Reforma.

blocks.en: Why this unit matters
blocks.es_reference: Por qué importa esta unidad

blocks.en: Unit 8 opened four Greek words from the Gospel of John: Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma. Unit 9 opens four more, this time from the Epistle to the Romans: pistis (faith), sôzô (save), dikaiosynê (righteousness), and kyrios (Lord). Together these eight nouns and verbs form the heart of the New Testament's salvation vocabulary. By the end of this unit you will be able to read Romans 1:16–17 in Greek — the verse that ignited the Reformation. You will see what Luther saw when he opened Erasmus's Greek Testament. Two more units after this: Unit 10 teaches you Strong's numbers in your hand, and Unit 11 turns you loose on your first real word study. You are about to cross the finish line.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 8 abrió cuatro palabras griegas del Evangelio de Juan: Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma. La Unidad 9 abre cuatro más, esta vez de la Epístola a los Romanos: pistis (fe), sôzô (salvar), dikaiosynê (justicia), y kyrios (Señor). Juntos estos ocho sustantivos y verbos forman el corazón del vocabulario de salvación del Nuevo Testamento. Al final de esta unidad podrás leer Romanos 1:16–17 en griego — el versículo que encendió la Reforma. Verás lo que Lutero vio cuando abrió el Nuevo Testamento griego de Erasmo. Dos unidades más después de esta: la Unidad 10 te enseña los números de Strong en la mano, y la Unidad 11 te suelta en tu primer estudio real de palabras. Estás a punto de cruzar la meta.

blocks.en: Notice that our unit scripture — Romans 1:16–17 — contains all four of the words we will study tonight. Paul packs them into two verses: sôtêria (salvation, the noun-form of sôzô), pisteuonti (believing, the verb-form of pistis), dikaiosynê, and pistis again. The whole Reformation is hidden in two verses, and the key to the safe is four Greek words.
blocks.es_reference: Nota que nuestra escritura — Romanos 1:16–17 — contiene las cuatro palabras que estudiaremos esta noche. Pablo las empaca en dos versículos: sôtêria (salvación, forma sustantiva de sôzô), pisteuonti (creyente, forma verbal de pistis), dikaiosynê, y pistis de nuevo. Toda la Reforma está escondida en dos versículos, y la llave de la caja fuerte son cuatro palabras griegas.

blocks.en: I. PISTIS (πίστις) — Faith That Trusts, Not Faith That Wishes
blocks.es_reference: I. PISTIS (πίστις) — Fe que confía, no fe que desea

blocks.en: faith, trust, reliance, conviction founded on what is trustworthy
blocks.es_reference: fe, confianza, dependencia, convicción fundada en lo que es digno de confianza

blocks.en: Modern English has done to the word "faith" what time did to "charity." It has shrunk it. Today when people say "I have faith," they often mean "I hope it works out." Faith has become a synonym for optimism with no object. "Just have faith." Faith in what? It doesn't matter; just have it. Believe in believing.
blocks.es_reference: El español moderno ha hecho con la palabra «fe» lo que el tiempo hizo con «caridad». La ha encogido. Hoy cuando la gente dice «tengo fe», a menudo significa «espero que salga bien». La fe se ha convertido en sinónimo de optimismo sin objeto. «Solo ten fe». ¿Fe en qué? No importa; solo tenla. Cree en creer.

blocks.en: The Greek word pistis never means anything close to that. Pistis is trust placed in something or someone trustworthy. Pistis without an object is not pistis at all. It is wishing. The Greek word always asks: trust in whom? In what? The trustworthiness of the object is the whole point of the faith. A chair I have never seen will hold me if it is well-built, regardless of how much pistis I bring to the act of sitting. A chair made of rotten wood will collapse under me no matter how much pistis I summon. Pistis is not the power that makes the chair hold. Pistis is the act of sitting on a chair that already holds. Christianity is not faith in faith. Christianity is faith in Christ.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra griega pistis nunca significa nada parecido a eso. Pistis es confianza puesta en algo o alguien digno de confianza. Pistis sin objeto no es pistis en absoluto. Es desear. La palabra griega siempre pregunta: ¿confianza en quién? ¿En qué? La fidelidad del objeto es todo el punto de la fe. Una silla que nunca he visto me sostendrá si está bien construida, sin importar cuánta pistis traiga al acto de sentarme. Una silla hecha de madera podrida se desplomará bajo mí sin importar cuánta pistis convoque. Pistis no es el poder que hace que la silla sostenga. Pistis es el acto de sentarse en una silla que ya sostiene. El cristianismo no es fe en la fe. El cristianismo es fe en Cristo.

blocks.en: The Hebrews 11 hall of fame
blocks.es_reference: El salón de la fama de Hebreos 11

blocks.en: Read Hebrews 11 in any English Bible and you find the word "faith" repeated like a drumbeat. "By faith Abel offered … By faith Enoch was translated … By faith Noah … By faith Abraham …" Every one of these is the same Greek word: pistei, the instrumental form of pistis. The entire chapter is a one-word chapter, repeated twenty-four times. And in every single case the faith has a definite object. Abel trusted God's instruction about sacrifice. Noah trusted God's warning about the flood. Abraham trusted God's promise of a son. Faith is never a vague feeling; it is always a response to a word from God. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17). The Greek confirms it: pistis ex akoês. Faith out of hearing. Faith needs an object, and the object is what God has actually said.
blocks.es_reference: Lee Hebreos 11 en cualquier Biblia y encuentras la palabra «fe» repetida como un tambor. «Por la fe Abel ofreció … Por la fe Enoc fue traspuesto … Por la fe Noé … Por la fe Abraham …» Cada uno de estos es la misma palabra griega: pistei, la forma instrumental de pistis. Todo el capítulo es un capítulo de una sola palabra, repetida veinticuatro veces. Y en cada caso la fe tiene un objeto definido. Abel confió en la instrucción de Dios sobre el sacrificio. Noé confió en la advertencia de Dios sobre el diluvio. Abraham confió en la promesa de Dios de un hijo. La fe nunca es un sentimiento vago; siempre es una respuesta a una palabra de Dios. La fe viene por el oír, y el oír por la palabra de Dios (Romanos 10:17). El griego lo confirma: pistis ex akoês. Fe a partir de oír. La fe necesita un objeto, y el objeto es lo que Dios ha dicho.

blocks.en: You will sometimes hear people say, "I just need to have more faith." That is the wrong question. The right question is: am I trusting the right Person about the right promise? Pistis is not measured by intensity. Pistis is measured by its object. The smallest pistis in the right Object saves; the largest pistis in the wrong object damns.
blocks.es_reference: A veces oirás a la gente decir: «Solo necesito tener más fe». Esa es la pregunta equivocada. La pregunta correcta es: ¿estoy confiando en la Persona correcta sobre la promesa correcta? Pistis no se mide por la intensidad. Pistis se mide por su objeto. La pistis más pequeña en el Objeto correcto salva; la pistis más grande en el objeto equivocado condena.

blocks.en: Faith and the verb pisteuô
blocks.es_reference: La fe y el verbo pisteuô

blocks.en: The noun pistis has a matching verb: pisteuô, "to believe, to trust." When John 3:16 says "whosoever believeth in Him," the Greek word is pisteuôn. Same root. So whenever you read either "faith" or "believe" in the English New Testament, you are usually looking at the same Greek family. Faith is something you have; believing is what you do with it. In Greek they are not two separate ideas. They are the noun and verb of one reality — trust placed in the trustworthy Christ.
blocks.es_reference: El sustantivo pistis tiene un verbo correspondiente: pisteuô, «creer, confiar». Cuando Juan 3:16 dice «todo aquel que en él cree», la palabra griega es pisteuôn. Misma raíz. Así que cada vez que leas «fe» o «creer» en el Nuevo Testamento castellano, usualmente estás viendo la misma familia griega. La fe es algo que tienes; creer es lo que haces con ella. En griego no son dos ideas separadas. Son el sustantivo y el verbo de una sola realidad — confianza puesta en el Cristo digno de confianza.

blocks.en: II. SÔZÔ (σωζω) — A Verb Bigger Than You Think
blocks.es_reference: II. SÔZÔ (σωζω) — Un verbo más grande de lo que crees

blocks.en: to save, rescue, deliver, heal, make whole, preserve, keep safe
blocks.es_reference: salvar, rescatar, librar, sanar, hacer entero, preservar, guardar a salvo

blocks.en: Ask the average Christian what "saved" means, and the answer is almost always: "saved from hell, going to heaven." That is true, but it is one-quarter true. The Greek verb sôzô is much bigger than that. It is one of the most flexible verbs in the New Testament, and it shows up in some surprising places.
blocks.es_reference: Pregúntale al cristiano promedio qué significa «salvo», y la respuesta es casi siempre: «salvo del infierno, yendo al cielo». Eso es verdad, pero es un cuarto de la verdad. El verbo griego sôzô es mucho más grande que eso. Es uno de los verbos más flexibles del Nuevo Testamento, y aparece en algunos lugares sorprendentes.

blocks.en: Sôzô means to rescue from danger, in any sense. It can rescue from drowning (Matthew 14:30, when Peter cries "Lord, save me" as he sinks — kyrie sôson me). It can rescue from disease (Mark 5:34, when Jesus tells the woman with the issue of blood, "your faith has made you whole" — hê pistis sou sesôken se; literally "your faith has saved you"). It can rescue from death (Mark 5:23, when Jairus begs Jesus to come heal his daughter "that she may be saved and live"). It can rescue from a sinking ship (Acts 27:31). And it can rescue from sin and judgment (Acts 16:31, when Paul tells the Philippian jailer, "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved").
blocks.es_reference: Sôzô significa rescatar del peligro, en cualquier sentido. Puede rescatar de ahogarse (Mateo 14:30, cuando Pedro clama «Señor, sálvame» mientras se hunde — kyrie sôson me). Puede rescatar de la enfermedad (Marcos 5:34, cuando Jesús le dice a la mujer con el flujo de sangre «tu fe te ha hecho salva» — hê pistis sou sesôken se; literalmente «tu fe te ha salvado»). Puede rescatar de la muerte (Marcos 5:23, cuando Jairo suplica a Jesús que venga a sanar a su hija «para que sea salva y viva»). Puede rescatar de un barco que se hunde (Hechos 27:31). Y puede rescatar del pecado y el juicio (Hechos 16:31, cuando Pablo le dice al carcelero de Filipos: «Cree en el Señor Jesucristo, y serás salvo»).

blocks.en: The Greek word does not split into "physical rescue" and "spiritual rescue." It holds them together. When the New Testament says Christ came to save, it means He came to rescue the whole person from every kind of ruin — from sin, from death, from sickness, from fear, from meaninglessness, from the grave itself. Salvation is comprehensive. Your soul is saved now. Your body will be saved at the resurrection. Your tears will be wiped away forever. Sôzô covers all of it.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra griega no se divide en «rescate físico» y «rescate espiritual». Los mantiene juntos. Cuando el Nuevo Testamento dice que Cristo vino a salvar, significa que vino a rescatar a la persona entera de toda clase de ruina — del pecado, de la muerte, de la enfermedad, del miedo, del sinsentido, de la tumba misma. La salvación es integral. Tu alma es salva ahora. Tu cuerpo será salvo en la resurrección. Tus lágrimas serán enjugadas para siempre. Sôzô cubre todo eso.

blocks.en: The English derivatives
blocks.es_reference: Los derivados en español

blocks.en: The Greek noun for "salvation" is sôtêria. The word for "savior" is sôtêr. These show up in English in unexpected places. Soteriology is the theological term for the doctrine of salvation. Soter is a common name in Greek Christian families to this day. And every Spanish-speaking Christian who has ever sung "Salvador mío" is calling on the sôtêr.
blocks.es_reference: El sustantivo griego para «salvación» es sôtêria. La palabra para «salvador» es sôtêr. Aparecen en español en lugares inesperados. Soteriología es el término teológico para la doctrina de la salvación. Sóter es un nombre común en familias cristianas griegas hasta el día de hoy. Y cada cristiano hispanohablante que ha cantado alguna vez «Salvador mío» está invocando al sôtêr.

blocks.en: Three tenses of salvation: I have been saved (justification, from sin's penalty). I am being saved (sanctification, from sin's power). I will be saved (glorification, from sin's presence). All three are sôzô. One Greek verb, three tenses, one Salvation.
blocks.es_reference: Tres tiempos de la salvación: He sido salvo (justificación, de la pena del pecado). Estoy siendo salvo (santificación, del poder del pecado). Seré salvo (glorificación, de la presencia del pecado). Los tres son sôzô. Un verbo griego, tres tiempos, una Salvación.

blocks.en: How this changes Bible reading
blocks.es_reference: Cómo esto cambia la lectura bíblica

blocks.en: When you read "He saves to the uttermost them that come unto God by Him" (Hebrews 7:25), the Greek is sôzein eis to panteles — "save unto the uttermost," "save completely." There is no half-saving with Christ. The verb in Greek is comprehensive, present-tense, ongoing. He saves and He keeps saving. The same Greek verb that rescued Peter from the waves is the verb that rescues you from your sin. The Carpenter of Galilee still reaches into storms.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando lees «Él puede salvar perpetuamente a los que por él se acercan a Dios» (Hebreos 7:25), el griego es sôzein eis to panteles — «salvar hasta lo último», «salvar completamente». No hay media salvación con Cristo. El verbo en griego es integral, en tiempo presente, continuo. Él salva y sigue salvando. El mismo verbo griego que rescató a Pedro de las olas es el verbo que te rescata a ti de tu pecado. El Carpintero de Galilea todavía alcanza dentro de las tormentas.

blocks.en: III. DIKAIOSYNÊ (δικαιοσυνη) — The Word That Lit the Reformation
blocks.es_reference: III. DIKAIOSYNÊ (δικαιοσυνη) — La palabra que encendió la Reforma

blocks.en: righteousness, justice, the right standing God gives by grace through faith
blocks.es_reference: justicia, rectitud, la posición correcta que Dios da por gracia mediante la fe

blocks.en: Greek dikaiosynê belongs to a whole family of related words. The adjective dikaios means "righteous" or "just." The verb dikaioô means "to declare righteous, to justify." The noun dikaiosynê means "righteousness" or "justification." The whole legal vocabulary of the doctrine of justification by faith hangs on this single Greek root.
blocks.es_reference: El griego dikaiosynê pertenece a toda una familia de palabras relacionadas. El adjetivo dikaios significa «justo» o «recto». El verbo dikaioô significa «declarar justo, justificar». El sustantivo dikaiosynê significa «justicia» o «justificación». Todo el vocabulario legal de la doctrina de la justificación por la fe cuelga de esta sola raíz griega.

blocks.en: Here is the problem Paul faced. In Greek and Roman thought, dikaiosynê meant moral excellence — the quality of being just, the standard of right conduct. A righteous person was a person whose life met the standard. By that definition, no one could be righteous before God. The Old Testament makes the case plainly: "There is none righteous, no, not one" (Romans 3:10, quoting Psalm 14). The standard is unmeetable. Pagan Greeks knew it. Pious Jews knew it. Luther knew it. Every honest soul who has ever read the Sermon on the Mount has known it.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí está el problema que Pablo enfrentó. En el pensamiento griego y romano, dikaiosynê significaba excelencia moral — la cualidad de ser justo, el estándar de la conducta recta. Una persona justa era una persona cuya vida cumplía el estándar. Por esa definición, nadie podría ser justo ante Dios. El Antiguo Testamento lo plantea claramente: «No hay justo, ni aun uno» (Romanos 3:10, citando Salmo 14). El estándar es inalcanzable. Los griegos paganos lo sabían. Los judíos piadosos lo sabían. Lutero lo sabía. Toda alma honesta que haya leído alguna vez el Sermón del Monte lo ha sabido.

blocks.en: What Paul does with the word
blocks.es_reference: Lo que hace Pablo con la palabra

blocks.en: And then Paul takes the word and does to it exactly what he did to charis. He flips it. In Romans 3 he announces "the dikaiosynê of God revealed apart from law … even the dikaiosynê of God by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe." Dikaiosynê in Paul is no longer the moral excellence you have to achieve. Dikaiosynê is the right standing God gives as a gift to those who trust in Christ. The verb dikaioô is a courtroom verb: it means "to declare righteous," to issue a verdict of "not guilty" from the bench. When God justifies the sinner who trusts Christ, He is not pretending the sinner is good. He is transferring Christ's perfect righteousness to the sinner's account and declaring the legal verdict: righteous.
blocks.es_reference: Y entonces Pablo toma la palabra y le hace exactamente lo que le hizo a charis. La invierte. En Romanos 3 anuncia «la dikaiosynê de Dios revelada aparte de la ley … la dikaiosynê de Dios por la fe de Jesucristo, para todos y sobre todos los que creen». Dikaiosynê en Pablo ya no es la excelencia moral que tienes que lograr. Dikaiosynê es la posición correcta que Dios da como un regalo a los que confían en Cristo. El verbo dikaioô es un verbo de tribunal: significa «declarar justo», emitir un veredicto de «no culpable» desde el estrado. Cuando Dios justifica al pecador que confía en Cristo, no está fingiendo que el pecador es bueno. Está transfiriendo la justicia perfecta de Cristo a la cuenta del pecador y declarando el veredicto legal: justo.

blocks.en: Christ took our sin on the cross; we receive His dikaiosynê by faith. This is called "the great exchange," and the whole transaction depends on one Greek word.
blocks.es_reference: Cristo tomó nuestro pecado en la cruz; nosotros recibimos Su dikaiosynê por la fe. Esto se llama «el gran intercambio», y toda la transacción depende de una palabra griega.

blocks.en: The Wittenberg tower revisited
blocks.es_reference: La torre de Wittenberg revisitada

blocks.en: Now go back to Luther in his study. The Latin Bible he had used all his life translated dikaiosynê as justitia, "justice." But the Latin word, by the year 1515, had drifted to mean the punitive justice of a judge — the standard by which God condemns. When Luther opened Erasmus's freshly printed Greek New Testament in 1516 and read Romans 1:17, he saw something the Latin had hidden: dikaiosynê theou is not the standard God demands. It is the gift God gives. "The just shall live by faith" — ho dikaios ek pisteôs zêsetai. Luther later wrote: "I felt myself to be born anew and to enter through open gates into paradise itself." That sentence, in the tower at Wittenberg, was the spark of the Reformation. One Greek word. One reformer's understanding. Half a millennium of Protestant history.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora regresa a Lutero en su estudio. La Biblia latina que había usado toda su vida traducía dikaiosynê como justitia, «justicia». Pero la palabra latina, para el año 1515, había derivado a significar la justicia punitiva de un juez — el estándar por el cual Dios condena. Cuando Lutero abrió el Nuevo Testamento griego recién impreso de Erasmo en 1516 y leyó Romanos 1:17, vio algo que el latín había escondido: dikaiosynê theou no es el estándar que Dios exige. Es el regalo que Dios da. «El justo por la fe vivirá» — ho dikaios ek pisteôs zêsetai. Lutero escribió después: «Me sentí nacido de nuevo y entrando por puertas abiertas al paraíso mismo». Esa oración, en la torre de Wittenberg, fue la chispa de la Reforma. Una palabra griega. La comprensión de un reformador. Medio milenio de historia protestante.

blocks.en: The English derivatives
blocks.es_reference: Los derivados en español

blocks.en: The Latin form justitia gives us English justice, justify, justification. The Greek dikaios gives us less directly — theodicy ("the justification of God," literally "God-justice"). (The proper name Eudokia, common in the Eastern Church, sounds related but is not: it means "good pleasure" and comes from a different root.) Whenever you see "justify" in an English Bible, think dikaioô. The legal verb. God's verdict, pronounced from the bench, transferring Christ's perfect record onto the sinner who trusts Him.
blocks.es_reference: La forma latina justitia nos da las palabras justicia, justificar, justificación. El griego dikaios nos da menos directamente — teodicea («la justificación de Dios», literalmente «Dios-justicia»). (El nombre propio Eudokia, común en la Iglesia Oriental, parece emparentado pero no lo es: significa «beneplácito» y viene de otra raíz.) Cada vez que veas «justificar» en una Biblia castellana, piensa dikaioô. El verbo legal. El veredicto de Dios, pronunciado desde el estrado, transfiriendo el registro perfecto de Cristo sobre el pecador que confía en Él.

blocks.en: IV. KYRIOS (κύριος) — The Title That Cost Roman Lives
blocks.es_reference: IV. KYRIOS (κύριος) — El título que costó vidas romanas

blocks.en: lord, master, owner, sovereign — the standard Greek title for God in the LXX and for Christ in the NT
blocks.es_reference: señor, amo, dueño, soberano — el título griego estándar para Dios en la LXX y para Cristo en el NT

blocks.en: The Greek word kyrios had two great uses in the first century, and the Christians took the second one and made it the defining confession of the church. Use one: any master or owner. A slave called his owner kyrios. A wife sometimes called her husband kyrios. A polite shopper in the agora called any unfamiliar man kyrios in the same way an English speaker says "sir." This is the lowest register of the word. Use two: the absolute Lord, the Sovereign of the universe. When the seventy translators rendered the Hebrew Old Testament into Greek around 250 BC (the Septuagint or LXX, which we met in Unit 2), they faced the question of how to translate the unspeakable divine Name, YHWH. Hebrew tradition refused to pronounce it; the rabbis substituted Adonai ("Lord") in reading. The Septuagint translators chose the equivalent Greek title: Kyrios. From 250 BC onward, every Greek-speaking Jew read his Old Testament with the word Kyrios standing in the place of God's covenant Name. Kyrios, in the Bible, is the name of God.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra griega kyrios tenía dos grandes usos en el primer siglo, y los cristianos tomaron el segundo y lo convirtieron en la confesión definitoria de la iglesia. Uso uno: cualquier amo o dueño. Un esclavo llamaba kyrios a su dueño. Una esposa a veces llamaba kyrios a su esposo. Un comprador cortés en el ágora llamaba kyrios a cualquier hombre desconocido de la misma manera en que un hablante de español dice «señor». Este es el registro más bajo de la palabra. Uso dos: el Señor absoluto, el Soberano del universo. Cuando los setenta traductores vertieron el Antiguo Testamento hebreo al griego alrededor del 250 a.C. (la Septuaginta o LXX, que conocimos en la Unidad 2), enfrentaron la pregunta de cómo traducir el Nombre divino impronunciable, YHWH. La tradición hebrea se negaba a pronunciarlo; los rabinos sustituían Adonai («Señor») al leer. Los traductores de la Septuaginta eligieron el título griego equivalente: Kyrios. Desde el 250 a.C. en adelante, todo judío de habla griega leyendo su Antiguo Testamento veía la palabra Kyrios en el lugar del Nombre del pacto de Dios. Kyrios, en la Biblia, es el nombre de Dios.

blocks.en: The Roman provocation
blocks.es_reference: La provocación romana

blocks.en: Now jump forward three centuries. In Rome under Domitian (the same emperor who exiled John to Patmos in Unit 7), the imperial cult began demanding that every Roman citizen affirm Kyrios Kaisar — "Caesar is Lord." It was a one-sentence loyalty test. Pinch a pinch of incense on the altar of the emperor's image and say three words: Kyrios Kaisar. Walk away free. Refuse, and you went to the lions. For most Romans the test was trivial — just a civic ritual, no deep belief required. For Christians it was impossible. They had already confessed three other words: Kyrios Iêsous. "Jesus is Lord."
blocks.es_reference: Ahora salta tres siglos adelante. En Roma bajo Domiciano (el mismo emperador que exilió a Juan a Patmos en la Unidad 7), el culto imperial comenzó a exigir que cada ciudadano romano afirmara Kyrios Kaisar — «César es Señor». Era una prueba de lealtad de una sola frase. Toma una pizca de incienso en el altar de la imagen del emperador y di tres palabras: Kyrios Kaisar. Sigue libre. Niégate, y vas a los leones. Para la mayoría de los romanos la prueba era trivial — solo un ritual cívico, sin creencia profunda requerida. Para los cristianos era imposible. Ya habían confesado otras tres palabras: Kyrios Iêsous. «Jesús es Señor».

blocks.en: Notice what is happening. The Christians are not using a generic word for "boss." They are taking the same Greek word the Septuagint used for YHWH and saying: that Person, the One the Old Testament calls Kyrios, is Jesus of Nazareth. The earliest Christian creed in the New Testament is three Greek words: Kyrios Iêsous, "Jesus is Lord" (1 Corinthians 12:3, Romans 10:9, Philippians 2:11). The shortest possible confession of faith. The word Kyrios attached to the name Jesus carries the full weight of Old Testament monotheism. To say "Jesus is Lord" is to say "Jesus is YHWH." And that is what the Romans heard. And that is why the Romans killed Christians.
blocks.es_reference: Nota lo que está sucediendo. Los cristianos no están usando una palabra genérica para «jefe». Están tomando la misma palabra griega que la Septuaginta usó para YHWH y diciendo: esa Persona, el Que el Antiguo Testamento llama Kyrios, es Jesús de Nazaret. El credo cristiano más temprano en el Nuevo Testamento son tres palabras griegas: Kyrios Iêsous, «Jesús es Señor» (1 Corintios 12:3, Romanos 10:9, Filipenses 2:11). La confesión de fe más corta posible. La palabra Kyrios unida al nombre Jesús carga todo el peso del monoteísmo del Antiguo Testamento. Decir «Jesús es Señor» es decir «Jesús es YHWH». Y eso fue lo que oyeron los romanos. Y por eso los romanos mataron a los cristianos.

blocks.en: Caesar wanted a pinch of incense. Christ asked for everything. The same word, kyrios, demanded an exclusive answer. Polycarp, Perpetua, Felicity, Justin, Lawrence, Ignatius — all chose the lions over the incense.
blocks.es_reference: El César quería una pizca de incienso. Cristo pidió todo. La misma palabra, kyrios, exigía una respuesta exclusiva. Policarpo, Perpetua, Felicidad, Justino, Lorenzo, Ignacio — todos eligieron los leones por encima del incienso.

blocks.en: The Philippians 2 hymn
blocks.es_reference: El himno de Filipenses 2

blocks.en: Philippians 2:9–11 contains the climactic Christian use of the word. Paul, quoting what may be an early Christian hymn, writes: "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Kyrios Iêsous Christos), to the glory of God the Father." That phrase — Kyrios Iêsous Christos — is the foundation creed of the Christian faith. The Greek word kyrios is the load-bearing wall. When you confess Jesus as Lord, you are not just saying He is your personal advisor. You are saying He is YHWH, the Sovereign of the universe, the One whose Name is above every name.
blocks.es_reference: Filipenses 2:9–11 contiene el uso climático cristiano de la palabra. Pablo, citando lo que puede ser un himno cristiano temprano, escribe: «Por lo cual Dios también le exaltó hasta lo sumo, y le dio un nombre que es sobre todo nombre; para que en el nombre de Jesús se doble toda rodilla de los que están en los cielos, y de los que en la tierra, y de los que debajo de la tierra; y toda lengua confiese que Jesucristo es el Señor (Kyrios Iêsous Christos), para la gloria de Dios Padre». Esa frase — Kyrios Iêsous Christos — es el credo fundacional de la fe cristiana. La palabra griega kyrios es la pared maestra. Cuando confiesas a Jesús como Señor, no solo estás diciendo que Él es tu consejero personal. Estás diciendo que Él es YHWH, el Soberano del universo, el Que tiene el Nombre que está sobre todo nombre.

blocks.en: The English and Spanish derivatives
blocks.es_reference: Los derivados en español

blocks.en: Through liturgical Greek, English picks up kyrie in the prayer Kyrie eleison, "Lord, have mercy," still sung in churches every Sunday around the world. Spanish has the word señor for everyday use and reserves it (capitalized as Señor) for Christ in the same way English reserves "Lord." Every time you sing "Christ is Lord" or "Cristo es el Señor," you are confessing what Polycarp went to the stake for. Kyrios Iêsous.
blocks.es_reference: A través del griego litúrgico, el español y el inglés recogen kyrie en la oración Kyrie eleison, «Señor, ten piedad», todavía cantada en iglesias cada domingo alrededor del mundo. El español tiene la palabra señor para uso cotidiano y la reserva (en mayúsculas como Señor) para Cristo de la misma manera que el inglés reserva «Lord». Cada vez que cantas «Cristo es el Señor» o «Christ is Lord», estás confesando aquello por lo que Policarpo fue a la hoguera. Kyrios Iêsous.

blocks.en: V. Reading Romans 1:16–17 in Greek
blocks.es_reference: V. Leyendo Romanos 1:16–17 en griego

blocks.en: You have now met eight Greek words. Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma from Unit 8; pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios from Unit 9. You are ready to read Luther's verse. Here is Romans 1:16–17 in transliterated Greek with English underneath:
blocks.es_reference: Ya has conocido ocho palabras griegas. Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma de la Unidad 8; pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios de la Unidad 9. Estás listo para leer el versículo de Lutero. Aquí está Romanos 1:16–17 en griego transliterado con español debajo:

blocks.en: Ou gar epaischynomai to euangelion · dynamis gar theou estin eis sôtêrian panti tôi pisteuonti …
blocks.es_reference: Ou gar epaischynomai to euangelion · dynamis gar theou estin eis sôtêrian panti tôi pisteuonti …

blocks.en: "For not I am ashamed of the gospel · power for of God it is unto salvation to everyone the believing …"
blocks.es_reference: «No porque me avergüenzo del evangelio · poder porque de Dios es para salvación a todo el creyente …»

blocks.en: dikaiosynê gar theou en autôi apokalyptetai ek pisteôs eis pistin · kathôs gegraptai · ho de dikaios ek pisteôs zêsetai.
blocks.es_reference: dikaiosynê gar theou en autôi apokalyptetai ek pisteôs eis pistin · kathôs gegraptai · ho de dikaios ek pisteôs zêsetai.

blocks.en: "righteousness for of God in it is revealed from faith unto faith · as it has been written · the now righteous from faith shall live."
blocks.es_reference: «justicia porque de Dios en él se revela de fe a fe · como está escrito · el ahora justo por fe vivirá».

blocks.en: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth … For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith."
blocks.es_reference: «Porque no me avergüenzo del evangelio de Cristo, porque es el poder de Dios para salvación a todo aquel que cree … Porque en el evangelio la justicia de Dios se revela de fe en fe, como está escrito: Mas el justo por la fe vivirá».

blocks.en: ROMANS 1:16–17 NKJV
blocks.es_reference: ROMANOS 1:16–17 RVG

blocks.en: Counting the words
blocks.es_reference: Contando las palabras

blocks.en: Read it again and count. Sôtêria (salvation, the noun-form of sôzô) appears once. Pisteuô (believing, the verb-form of pistis) appears once. Dikaiosynê (righteousness) appears once. Pistis (faith) appears three times. Kyrios is not in these two verses, but Christ is named: "the gospel of Christ" — and "Christ" in Pauline usage almost never travels without His Lordship implied. In two verses Paul has packed the salvation vocabulary of the Greek New Testament. This is why Luther could spend years on Romans and never reach the bottom. Every word is a doorway.
blocks.es_reference: Léelo de nuevo y cuenta. Sôtêria (salvación, forma sustantiva de sôzô) aparece una vez. Pisteuô (creyendo, forma verbal de pistis) aparece una vez. Dikaiosynê (justicia) aparece una vez. Pistis (fe) aparece tres veces. Kyrios no está en estos dos versículos, pero Cristo es nombrado: «el evangelio de Cristo» — y «Cristo» en el uso paulino casi nunca viaja sin Su Señorío implicado. En dos versículos Pablo ha empacado el vocabulario de salvación del Nuevo Testamento griego. Por eso Lutero pudo pasar años en Romanos y nunca tocar fondo. Cada palabra es una puerta.

blocks.en: What Luther saw
blocks.es_reference: Lo que Lutero vio

blocks.en: Now read it with Luther's eyes. The dikaiosynê of God is being revealed — not the standard God demands, but the gift God gives. From faith to faith (ek pisteôs eis pistin) — salvation begins in faith, continues in faith, ends in faith, faith from start to finish. The just shall live by faith — the Habakkuk 2:4 quotation that runs through Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews like the bass line of the entire New Testament. The just live by pistis. Not by works. Not by climbing stairs in Rome on bleeding knees. By pistis. By trust in the Kyrios.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora léelo con los ojos de Lutero. La dikaiosynê de Dios se está revelando — no el estándar que Dios exige, sino el regalo que Dios da. De fe en fe (ek pisteôs eis pistin) — la salvación empieza en fe, continúa en fe, termina en fe, fe de principio a fin. El justo por la fe vivirá — la cita de Habacuc 2:4 que corre por Romanos, Gálatas, y Hebreos como la línea de bajo de todo el Nuevo Testamento. El justo vive por pistis. No por obras. No por subir escaleras en Roma con rodillas sangrientas. Por pistis. Por confianza en el Kyrios.

blocks.en: When Luther understood these two verses in Greek, he later wrote: "Here I felt myself altogether born again, and to have gone through open doors into paradise itself." The Greek opened doors the Latin had hidden. The same doors are open to you tonight.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Lutero entendió estos dos versículos en griego, escribió después: «Aquí me sentí del todo nacido de nuevo, y que había pasado por puertas abiertas al paraíso mismo». El griego abrió puertas que el latín había escondido. Las mismas puertas están abiertas para ti esta noche.

blocks.en: Notebook activity
blocks.es_reference: Actividad de cuaderno

blocks.en: Before you take the examination, do this. Open the same notebook you used in Unit 8. Find the page where you wrote Logos, Agapê, Charis, Pneuma. Underneath, write Pistis, Sôzô, Dikaiosynê, Kyrios. For each one, write the English meaning, the verse you will remember it by, and one sentence describing how the Greek changes your reading. Now look at the whole page. Eight Greek words. Two columns. The Father, the Son, the Spirit, salvation, faith, righteousness, the Lord. You have the New Testament's salvation vocabulary on one page. Frame it. Tape it inside your study Bible. These eight words will travel with you the rest of your life.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de tomar el examen, haz esto. Abre el mismo cuaderno que usaste en la Unidad 8. Encuentra la página donde escribiste Logos, Agapê, Charis, Pneuma. Debajo, escribe Pistis, Sôzô, Dikaiosynê, Kyrios. Para cada una, escribe el significado en español, el versículo por el que la recordarás, y una oración describiendo cómo el griego cambia tu lectura. Ahora mira toda la página. Ocho palabras griegas. Dos columnas. El Padre, el Hijo, el Espíritu, la salvación, la fe, la justicia, el Señor. Tienes el vocabulario de salvación del Nuevo Testamento en una página. Enmárcala. Pégala dentro de tu Biblia de estudio. Estas ocho palabras viajarán contigo el resto de tu vida.

blocks.en: Where Unit 10 picks up
blocks.es_reference: Dónde retoma la Unidad 10

blocks.en: Unit 10 changes gears. Until now we have been opening words one at a time as Wayne points them out to you. In Unit 10 you learn the tool that lets you do this yourself for any word in the Bible: Strong's numbers. Every Hebrew and Greek word in the Bible is keyed to a number. G3056 is logos. G4982 is sôzô. G2962 is kyrios. With Strong's numbers in your hand, you can open the lid on any word in any verse, any time. Unit 10 teaches Strong's three ways: on paper (the original concordance), on a phone (the modern apps), and on the full internet (Bible study websites). Then Unit 11 turns you loose on your first real word study. Two units left. You can see the finish line.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 10 cambia de marcha. Hasta ahora hemos estado abriendo palabras una a la vez mientras Wayne te las señala. En la Unidad 10 aprendes la herramienta que te permite hacer esto tú mismo para cualquier palabra en la Biblia: los números de Strong. Cada palabra hebrea y griega de la Biblia está numerada. G3056 es logos. G4982 es sôzô. G2962 es kyrios. Con los números de Strong en la mano, puedes abrir la tapa de cualquier palabra en cualquier versículo, en cualquier momento. La Unidad 10 enseña Strong en tres formas: en papel (la concordancia original), en teléfono (las aplicaciones modernas), y en internet completo (sitios de estudio bíblico). Luego la Unidad 11 te suelta en tu primer estudio real de palabras. Dos unidades quedan. Puedes ver la meta.

mc.stem: In what year did Martin Luther read Erasmus's freshly printed Greek New Testament and finally understand the meaning of Romans 1:17?
mc.why: Erasmus published his Greek New Testament in 1516. Luther, preparing lectures on Romans in the Wittenberg tower around 1515–1517, opened the Greek and saw what the Latin justitia had hidden: dikaiosynê is the righteousness God gives, not the standard God demands. That moment lit the Reformation. The Ninety-Five Theses followed in October 1517.

mc.stem: What does the Greek word pistis NEVER mean in the New Testament?
options: A wish or vague optimism with no object
Trust placed in something or someone trustworthy
Conviction founded on what God has actually said
Reliance on the promises of Christ
mc.why: Pistis is never a vague wish. It is always trust placed in a trustworthy object. The trustworthiness of the object is the whole point of the faith. The smallest pistis in the right Object saves; the largest pistis in the wrong object damns. Modern English has shrunk 'faith' into 'optimism with no object,' but the Greek word never moves that direction.

mc.stem: In Hebrews 11 (the 'hall of faith' chapter), the phrase 'by faith' is repeated dozens of times. Each time it represents the same Greek word in instrumental form. What is the Greek root?
options: agapê
pneuma
dikaiosynê
pistis (instrumental: pistei)
mc.why: Every occurrence of 'by faith' in Hebrews 11 is the same Greek word pistis in instrumental form, pistei. The chapter is a one-word chapter repeated twenty-four times. And in every case the faith has a definite object: Abel trusted God about sacrifice, Noah about the flood, Abraham about the promised son. Pistis always has an object.

mc.stem: How does the Greek verb sôzô (to save) function in the New Testament?
options: It refers only to rescue from hell at final judgment
It is a flexible verb meaning to rescue from danger in any sense — from drowning, disease, death, shipwreck, or sin
It refers only to physical healing of disease
It refers only to escape from Roman persecution
mc.why: Sôzô is one of the most flexible verbs in the NT. It rescues Peter from drowning (Matthew 14:30), the woman from her hemorrhage (Mark 5:34), Jairus's daughter from death (Mark 5:23), Paul's ship from a storm (Acts 27:31), and the Philippian jailer from sin and judgment (Acts 16:31). The Greek refuses to split 'physical' from 'spiritual' rescue. Salvation is comprehensive.

mc.stem: What does the Greek noun sôtêr mean?
options: Healer of the body only
Teacher of doctrine
Savior — the One who rescues, the agent of sôzô
Builder of houses
mc.why: Sôtêr is the noun for Savior, the agent of the verb sôzô. Sôtêria is the noun for salvation. Soteriology is the theological term for the doctrine of salvation. Every Spanish-speaking Christian who sings 'Salvador mío' is calling on the sôtêr. The Greek family sôzô/sôtêr/sôtêria covers the whole vocabulary of rescue.

mc.stem: Theologians speak of three tenses of salvation. What are they?
options: Past, present, future — in only one of which I am actually saved
I have been saved (justification, from sin's penalty); I am being saved (sanctification, from sin's power); I will be saved (glorification, from sin's presence)
Saved by works, then by faith, then by grace — one tense per dispensation
Three different salvations — spiritual, physical, social
mc.why: All three tenses are the same Greek verb sôzô: 'I have been saved' (past, justification, freed from the penalty of sin); 'I am being saved' (present, sanctification, being freed from the power of sin); 'I will be saved' (future, glorification, will be freed from the very presence of sin in the resurrection). One Greek verb, three tenses, one comprehensive Salvation.

mc.stem: What is the Greek noun for 'righteousness' that Luther saw in Romans 1:17 in Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament?
options: sabbath
agapê
hesed
dikaiosynê
mc.why: Dikaiosynê is the Greek noun for righteousness. The adjective dikaios means 'just' or 'righteous.' The verb dikaioô means 'to declare righteous, to justify.' Together this family carries the entire vocabulary of justification by faith. Luther's breakthrough in the Wittenberg tower was realizing dikaiosynê theou (the righteousness of God) is the gift God gives, not the standard God demands.

mc.stem: Before Luther's breakthrough, how had he understood the Latin phrase 'justitia Dei' (justice/righteousness of God) in his Bible?
options: As the perfect moral standard by which God judges sinners and condemns them
As a free gift God grants apart from any human merit
As a Hebrew loan-word with no precise meaning
As a title for the Holy Spirit
mc.why: To Luther before his Greek breakthrough, justitia Dei meant the punitive standard by which God judges sinners guilty. He hated the verse and even said he hated God for putting it in the Bible. When he opened Erasmus's Greek and read dikaiosynê in the verb forms Paul actually used, he saw the righteousness was something God GIVES to those who believe, not the standard by which He CONDEMNS. The gates of paradise opened.

mc.stem: What does the Greek verb dikaioô mean in Paul's letters?
options: To make someone morally perfect by sinless living
To declare righteous — a courtroom verb meaning 'to issue a verdict of not guilty'
To examine the deeds of the dead at final judgment
To balance moral debits and credits in a heavenly ledger
mc.why: Dikaioô is a courtroom verb, not a transformation verb. It means to declare righteous, to issue a verdict of 'not guilty' from the bench. When God justifies the sinner who trusts Christ, He is not pretending the sinner is good. He is transferring Christ's perfect righteousness to the sinner's account and pronouncing the legal verdict: righteous. This is the foundation of the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone.

mc.stem: What is meant by 'the great exchange' in connection with dikaiosynê?
options: The trade of Hebrew names for Greek names among first-century Christians
The substitution of Greek philosophy for Hebrew theology in the early church
Christ took our sin on the cross; we receive His perfect righteousness (dikaiosynê) by faith
The conversion of Roman pagans into Christian believers
mc.why: The 'great exchange' is the heart of the gospel and depends entirely on the Greek word dikaiosynê. On the cross, Christ received the sinner's debt. By faith, the sinner receives Christ's perfect righteousness. 'He made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him' (2 Corinthians 5:21). My sin to Him, His righteousness to me. The whole transaction is contained in one Greek word.

mc.stem: How did the Septuagint translators (around 250 BC) render the Hebrew covenant name YHWH into Greek?
options: They left YHWH untranslated in Hebrew letters
They used Theos (God) every time
They invented a new Greek word with no prior history
They used Kyrios (Lord) — the same word the rabbis substituted in Hebrew reading with Adonai
mc.why: The Septuagint translators chose Kyrios for YHWH, paralleling the Hebrew tradition of reading Adonai instead of pronouncing the divine Name. From 250 BC onward, every Greek-speaking Jew read his Old Testament with Kyrios in the place of God's covenant Name. Kyrios in the Bible is the name of God. This is what the early Christians inherited when they confessed 'Kyrios Iêsous' — Jesus is YHWH.

mc.stem: What does the three-word confession 'Kyrios Iêsous' (Jesus is Lord) declare about Jesus?
options: That He was a respected first-century rabbi
That He is YHWH — the Sovereign of the universe, the One the Old Testament names with the covenant Name
That He is one helpful teacher among many ancient sages
That He gave good advice on personal finances
mc.why: Because the Septuagint used Kyrios for YHWH, when the earliest Christians confessed 'Kyrios Iêsous' they were saying 'Jesus is YHWH.' The shortest creed in the NT (1 Corinthians 12:3, Romans 10:9) carries the full weight of Old Testament monotheism. The Greek word kyrios is the load-bearing wall of the doctrine of the deity of Christ. And that is why the Romans killed Christians who would not say Kyrios Kaisar.

mc.stem: In the Roman Empire under Domitian and later emperors, what one-sentence loyalty test were Christians asked to affirm?
options: 'Caesar is divine, Christ is divine, both are good' — Roman pluralism
'I renounce all foreign religions' — nationalism only
'There are many gods' — pure polytheism
'Kyrios Kaisar' — Caesar is Lord
mc.why: Roman emperor-worship demanded the three-word confession Kyrios Kaisar — 'Caesar is Lord' — with a pinch of incense on the imperial altar. For most Romans the test was a trivial civic ritual. For Christians who had already confessed Kyrios Iêsous, it was impossible. The same Greek word, applied to two different lords, could not belong to both at once. Polycarp, Perpetua, Felicity, Justin, Ignatius, and thousands more chose the lions over the incense.

mc.stem: In which New Testament passage does Paul include the climactic confession 'Kyrios Iêsous Christos' (Jesus Christ is Lord), declaring that every knee will bow and every tongue confess this name?
options: Philippians 2:9–11
Genesis 1:1
Psalm 23
Revelation 22:21
mc.why: Philippians 2:9–11 is the great Christological climax: 'God hath given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow … and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Kyrios Iêsous Christos), to the glory of God the Father.' Paul may be quoting an even earlier Christian hymn. The phrase Kyrios Iêsous Christos is the foundation creed of the church.

mc.stem: Our unit scripture, Romans 1:16–17, contains how many of the four Greek words studied in Unit 9 (pistis, sôzô/sôtêria, dikaiosynê, kyrios)?
options: One only — pistis
Two — pistis and sôtêria
Three explicitly — sôtêria, pisteuô/pistis (multiple forms), and dikaiosynê (with kyrios implied in 'Christ')
None — the words appear elsewhere in Romans but not in these verses
mc.why: Romans 1:16–17 explicitly contains sôtêria (salvation), the verb pisteuô (believing, related to pistis), pistis itself (three times: 'from faith to faith … the just shall live by faith'), and dikaiosynê (righteousness). Kyrios is not in these two verses but is implied in 'the gospel of Christ' since 'Christ' in Pauline usage carries Lordship. Paul packs the salvation vocabulary of the entire New Testament into two verses.

mc.stem: In Romans 1:17, the Greek phrase 'ek pisteôs eis pistin' is translated 'from faith to faith.' What does it mean?
options: Salvation requires Old Testament Jewish faith first, then New Testament Christian faith second
Salvation is faith from start to finish — it begins in faith, continues in faith, and ends in faith
Faith must be exchanged between two believers like a handshake
Faith is partial and must be supplemented by works
mc.why: The phrase ek pisteôs eis pistin (literally 'out of faith into faith') means faith is the principle from start to finish. Salvation begins in faith (justification), continues in faith (sanctification), and ends in faith (glorification). The Habakkuk 2:4 quotation that follows — 'the just shall live by faith' — runs through Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews as the bass line of the entire New Testament's doctrine of salvation.

mc.stem: How are the noun pistis and the verb pisteuô related in Greek?
options: They are two completely unrelated Greek words with separate roots
Pistis is the noun ('faith') and pisteuô is the matching verb ('to believe, to trust') — same root, noun and verb of one reality
Pistis is Hebrew; pisteuô is Greek
Pistis is for the Old Testament; pisteuô is for the New
mc.why: Pistis (faith) and pisteuô (to believe, to trust) share the same Greek root. They are the noun and verb of one reality: trust placed in the trustworthy Christ. When John 3:16 says 'whosoever believeth in Him,' the Greek is pisteuôn — the active participle of pisteuô. Faith and believing are not two separate ideas in Greek. They are the still and moving forms of the same reality.

mc.stem: The eight Greek words across Units 8 and 9 form the salvation vocabulary of the New Testament. Which list is correct?
options: Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma + pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios
Aleph, beth, gimel, dalet + alpha, beta, gamma, delta
Hesed, shalom, ruach, dabar + nomos, sarx, kosmos, hamartia
Hosanna, hallelujah, amen, maranatha + abba, rabbi, eloi, talitha
mc.why: The eight words of Units 8 and 9 are: Logos (Word), agapê (love), charis (grace), pneuma (Spirit), pistis (faith), sôzô (save), dikaiosynê (righteousness), kyrios (Lord). Together they hold the New Testament's salvation vocabulary in one breath: the Person revealed, the love that sent Him, the grace He brings, the Spirit He gives, the faith that receives Him, the salvation He works, the righteousness He grants, the Lordship He claims.

mc.stem: What did Luther write about his experience when he finally understood the Greek dikaiosynê in Romans 1:17?
options: That he felt nothing in particular, since theology is a matter of cold reason
That he felt himself born anew, and entered through open gates into paradise itself
That he immediately destroyed the Greek New Testament as too dangerous to read
That he doubted whether the verse was original to Paul
mc.why: Luther later wrote: 'Here I felt myself altogether born again, and to have gone through open doors into paradise itself.' One Greek word — dikaiosynê — understood correctly, opened the gates of paradise to a tortured monk and ignited the Reformation. The Ninety-Five Theses followed in October 1517. Five hundred years of Protestant history flow from one man's careful reading of one verse in the original Greek.

mc.stem: What is the Strong's number for each of the four Unit 9 Greek words?
options: They are all assigned the same number G0000
Pistis G4102, sôzô G4982, dikaiosynê G1343, kyrios G2962
Greek words do not have Strong's numbers — only Hebrew words do
Strong's numbers were abolished in the 1900s and are no longer used
mc.why: Every Hebrew and Greek word in the Bible is keyed to a number in Strong's Exhaustive Concordance: G for Greek (1–5624), H for Hebrew (1–8674). Pistis is G4102, sôzô is G4982, dikaiosynê is G1343, kyrios is G2962. With Strong's numbers in your hand you can open the lid on any word in any verse. Unit 10 teaches you how to use them in three forms: paper, phone, and full internet.
